lines.say: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells, and cells come from cells.
Exchange happens at the surface, but the volume sets how much is needed.
A cube with 1 micrometre sides has a ratio of 6 to 1.

draw.alt: Small cube with high SA:V and large cube with low SA:V

lines.say: Make it 10 micrometres, and the ratio drops to 0.6 to 1.

draw.alt: Large cube added with much lower SA:V

lines.say: Big cells can't exchange fast enough, unless they're thin or folded.
Pro means no nucleus. The DNA sits in a region called the nucleoid.
Prokaryotes have 70 S ribosomes, often plasmids, and no membrane-bound organelles.

draw.alt: Bacterium with nucleoid, plasmid, ribosomes and flagellum

lines.say: Bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan. Archaea walls don't.
Eukaryotes have a nucleus with a double membrane and pores, and 80 S ribosomes.
Their organelles make compartments, so different reactions can run at once.
Think of a factory and post office. Follow one secreted protein.
A signal sequence docks the ribosome on the rough E R.
In the E R lumen it folds and gets its first sugars.
A vesicle carries it to the Golgi: in at the cis face, out at the trans face.

draw.alt: Rough ER to vesicle to Golgi to secretory vesicle to membrane

lines.say: A secretory vesicle fuses with the membrane. That's exocytosis.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are not part of this system.
Three fibres: microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules.
Actin gives shape and works with myosin in muscle.
Microtubules are the tracks. Kinesin kicks out, dynein drags in.
Cilia have a nine plus two pattern and bend. They never rotate.
Mitochondria came from an engulfed bacterium. Chloroplasts came from a cyanobacterium.
The bacterium was wrapped in host membrane. That explains two membranes.

draw.alt: Host membrane wraps a bacterium, giving a double membrane

lines.say: Two DNA Ribs Divide: two membranes, circular DNA, 70 S ribosomes, binary fission.
Add their bacterial size and rRNA sequences for full marks.
Image equals actual size times magnification.
An image is 36 millimetres at 18,000 times. Convert first: 36,000 micrometres.
Divide by 18,000. The mitochondrion is 2 micrometres long.
Resolution, not magnification, limits detail. Light microscopes reach about 200 nanometres.
Electron microscopes see much finer detail, but only in dead, fixed samples.
Prokaryotes have ribosomes. They just lack membrane-bound organelles.
Always convert to the same units before dividing.
Ribosome, rough E R, vesicle, Golgi, vesicle, membrane.
Bigger magnification past the limit just gives a bigger blur.
